articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities and Individuals in Iranian 'Shadow Banking' Network
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new sanctions on November 23, 2026, targeting individuals and entities involved in an Iranian 'shadow banking' network. This action is part of a broader effort to sever financial lifelines sustaining the Iranian regime.

The designations include eight Iranian citizens and several trading entities based in the United Arab Emirates, Turkey, and Hong Kong. Treasury described this network as the 'last financial lifeline of a bankrupt regime,' underscoring the significant impact of these sanctions on Iran's ability to access foreign currency and facilitate international trade.

These actions were taken under Executive Order (E.O.) 13902, which targets certain sectors of the Iranian economy, E.O. 13224, as amended, the United States' counterterrorism sanctions authority, and E.O. 13871, which targets persons operating in certain sectors of Iran's metals industry.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran Designations and New Cuba FAQs
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran designations on November 20, 2026, as part of 'Operation Economic Outcast,' targeting individuals involved in facilitating Iranian oil sales and supporting previously designated entities.

Specifically, Mohammad Javad Bavand and Majid Taj were designated pursuant to E.O. 13902 for operating in the petroleum sector of the Iranian economy. They are described as part of a network of regime insiders tasked with selling Iranian oil and recovering oil proceeds held in third countries.

In addition to the Iran-related actions, OFAC also issued new Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) concerning the Cuba sanctions program. These FAQs provide updated guidance on OFAC's regulations regarding Cuba.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements Counter Narcotics and Cyber-related Designations; Amends Russia-related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on November 19, 2026, targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and cyber-related illicit activities. This action underscores the U.S. government's commitment to disrupting global criminal networks.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued a new Illicit Drugs General License to facilitate certain transactions. This license aims to ensure that legitimate humanitarian and other authorized activities are not unduly impacted by the new sanctions.

Furthermore, OFAC issued an amended Russia-related General License and updated Frequently Asked Questions. This amendment reflects ongoing adjustments to the sanctions regime in response to evolving geopolitical circumstances and aims to provide clarity for compliance.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces New Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) implemented new counter terrorism designations on November 18, 2026. These actions are part of the ongoing U.S. strategy to combat global terrorism and disrupt financial support networks for terrorist organizations.

The specific individuals and entities targeted by these designations were not immediately detailed in the initial announcement but fall under the broader authority of U.S. counterterrorism sanctions programs. These measures aim to freeze assets and prohibit transactions with those identified as supporting terrorist activities.

These designations reinforce the U.S. government's commitment to using its financial tools to protect national security interests and prevent the flow of funds to groups that pose a threat to international stability.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities in Joint Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Action
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on November 13, 2026, targeting entities involved in both counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities. This joint action highlights the interconnectedness of various illicit networks and the comprehensive approach taken by the U.S. government to combat them.

These designations aim to disrupt the financial and operational capabilities of organizations that engage in drug trafficking and simultaneously support terrorist groups. The specific details of the designated entities were not immediately released but are subject to asset freezes and prohibitions on transactions with U.S. persons.

This action is consistent with OFAC's mandate to protect the U.S. financial system from abuse by illicit actors and to safeguard national security interests by targeting those who pose a threat through their involvement in both narcotics and terrorism.

body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) published an Iran Designation Update on November 9, 2026. This update provides additional information or modifications to existing Iran-related designations.

Such updates are routine as OFAC continuously monitors and adjusts its sanctions lists to reflect new intelligence and evolving circumstances. The specific nature of this update, whether additions, removals, or modifications to existing entries, was not detailed in the initial announcement.

These sanctions aim to disrupt the flow of funds and resources to entities and individuals supporting Iran's destabilizing activities. The specific targets of these designations were not immediately detailed in the announcement but fall under the broader scope of U.S. sanctions against Iran.
This action reinforces the U.S. government's commitment to applying maximum pressure on Iran to curb its illicit activities and prevent its access to the international financial system.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements Cyber-related and Transnational Criminal Organizations Designations; Cuba Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on November 5, 2026, targeting cyber-related illicit activities and transnational criminal organizations.

In a significant development, OFAC also implemented new Cuba designations, including Chinese companies for the first time, for their involvement in the transport of crude oil and other petroleum products to the island.

These Cuba-related actions also targeted other Cuban state enterprises, such as CUBAELECTRONICA, which imports electronics, and TECNOSIME, involved in metalworking. This marks an escalation of economic pressure on Cuba.

In conjunction with these actions, OFAC published an Iran-related OFAC Alert, likely providing guidance on sanctions evasion tactics or specific risks. This alert aims to enhance awareness and compliance within the financial and maritime sectors.

Additionally, OFAC issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a corresponding Frequently Asked Question. This amendment reflects ongoing adjustments to the U.S. sanctions policy towards Venezuela, which has seen easing through licenses since early 2026.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Iran-related General License on October 29, 2026. This amendment modifies existing authorizations for certain transactions involving Iran.

General Licenses are issued to authorize categories of transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under sanctions programs. The specific details of this amendment were not immediately available but are intended to provide clarity or adjust the scope of permissible activities.
Such amendments are part of OFAC's dynamic approach to sanctions implementation, balancing enforcement with humanitarian considerations or other policy objectives.

articles.headline: EU Restricts Trade with 15 Entities Linked to Russia's Military-Industrial Complex
body: On November 25, 2026, the Council of the European Union decided to add 15 Russian entities to the list of those subject to tighter export restrictions on dual-use goods and advanced technologies. These entities are identified as part of Russia's military and industrial complex, with links to or support for Russia's defense and security sector.

This decision aligns with the EU's commitment to increasing pressure on Russia to halt its war of aggression against Ukraine. The tighter export restrictions aim to impede Russia's ability to acquire sensitive goods that could contribute to its war effort.

The Council also decided to remove one entity from the list, citing that the entity had ceased the behavior that led to its listing and provided credible assurances against trading sensitive goods with Russia.

articles.headline: UK Updates Sanctions List for Democratic People's Republic of Korea
body: On November 17, 2026, the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office updated the UK Sanctions List on GOV.UK with a variation to the designation of Mansudae Overseas Project Group of Companies.

The update provides additional information regarding the entity, which is designated under the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (Sanctions) (EU Exit) Regulations 2019. Mansudae Overseas Project Group of Companies is identified as being involved in the exportation of workers from the DPRK to other nations for construction-related activities, including statues and monuments, to generate revenue for the Government of the DPRK or the Workers' Party of Korea.

The company has reportedly conducted business in various countries in Africa and Southeast Asia. The sanctions imposed include asset freezes, chartering of ships, closure of representative offices, crew servicing of ships and aircraft, prevention of business arrangements, and prohibition of port entry.

articles.headline: BIS Adds Seven Entities in Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand to Entity List
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amended the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by adding seven entities to the Entity List, effective November 23, 2026. These entities are located in Malaysia (three), Singapore (three), and Thailand (one).

The U.S. Government determined that these entities pose a significant risk of being involved in activities contrary to the national security or foreign policy interests of the United States, specifically the diversion of advanced computing commodities to unauthorized end uses or end users.

For each newly listed entity, a license is now required for all items subject to the EAR, and license applications will be reviewed under a presumption of denial. A savings clause allows certain shipments already en route on November 23, 2026, to proceed to their destination if completed by December 23, 2026.

articles.headline: European Commission Approves Over 20 Investments to Boost Semiconductor Supply, Totaling €33 Billion
body: On November 17, 2026, the European Commission announced a major milestone under the second pillar of the European Chips Act, approving more than 20 State aid decisions for first-of-a-kind semiconductor facilities. These approvals have unlocked over €33 billion in combined public and private investment.

These investments span the entire semiconductor value chain, from wafers and chips to advanced packaging, testing, assembly, specialized materials, and power electronics. The initiative aims to strengthen and diversify Europe's position in the semiconductor ecosystem and reduce strategic dependencies.

The European Chips Act is designed to boost Europe's sovereignty and competitiveness in semiconductor technologies through three pillars of action. These decisions are expected to stimulate wider economic activity across the EU while advancing the Union's technological sovereignty goals.

articles.headline: Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors
body: In this interim final rule (IFR), the Department of Commerce is establishing new rules to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. First, this rule establishes new restrictions which will apply for exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) to overseas data centers that remotely supply significant volumes of compute to companies headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau. These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models. Data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exporters are required to perform robust due diligence on their customers, including any direct or indirect ownership or control by persons in Country Group D:5 or Macau, as part of complying with this new control. The license requirement will not apply to commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat. Second, in addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, a license will be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs)--countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. The license requirement for these five countries will not apply to semiconductors destined to companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, the United States, provided certain reporting requirements are met. Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion of this IFR and will consider a range of consequences for such countries, such as import restrictions, new license requirements on advanced semiconductor exports, downgrading the country's status in the U.S. export control regime, and Entity List designations and temporary export prohibitions for foreign persons involved in such activities. Third, this IFR amends the presumptions which front-end chips fabricators and chip packagers face when exporting advanced-node logic chips. These amendments reduce the number of pathways to overcome the presumptions for chip designers located in destinations which face a license requirement for SI chips. This change gives the U.S. government critical oversight over companies headquartered in certain countries that seek to leverage advanced semiconductor production capabilities in third countries. Finally, the IFR formally rescinds the regulations implementing the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. The AI Diffusion Rule has never been enforced. The regulatory changes in this rule formalize the rescission of the AI Diffusion Rule, which the Department of Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced in May 2025.

articles.headline: Extension of the Suspension of Expansion of End-User Controls for Affiliates of Certain Listed Entities
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is extending the suspension of the interim final rule (IFR), "Expansion of End-User Controls to Cover Affiliates of Certain Listed Entities." The suspension was set to end November 9, 2026. This final rule extends the suspension through January 10, 2027.

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
